title: Patterns of use and harm reduction practices of ecstasy users in Australia

claims.statement: Among 116 adults in Australia who had used ecstasy at least once, surveyed in 2004 through the researchers' acquaintances and their networks and through an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (Allott & Redman, 2006; 51 in 100 women, mean age 26.5), every respondent reported at least one thing they did to avoid ecstasy's negative side effects, chosen from a list: most often drinking water (96 in 100), limiting the amount of ecstasy (71 in 100), taking breaks or chilling out (62 in 100), a healthy lifestyle (60 in 100) and vitamins or natural products (53 in 100); 30 in 100 took other illegal drugs and 16 in 100 prescription medicines for this. To avoid the comedown in the days after, 4 in 100 had no strategy, and to avoid brain damage, 18 in 100 had none. 41 in 100 had taken pharmaceuticals or natural products before ecstasy ('preloading') and 47 in 100 after it ('postloading'): among those who listed them, half took multivitamins and 41 in 100 took 5-HTP (a building block of serotonin) before, followed by magnesium and fruit or juice, and 46 in 100 took 5-HTP and 44 in 100 multivitamins after; among those who gave reasons, 46 in 100 did it to ease the comedown and 33 in 100 to reduce brain damage. About 39 in 100 had ever tested their pills (61 in 100 never had; editors' calculation), and 53 in 100 had changed how they used ecstasy because of something they disliked about it, most of them by using it less often. Every respondent had also used at least one other substance with ecstasy, most often alcohol (91 in 100 before and 81 in 100 during use) and amphetamines (60 in 100 before and 66 in 100 during). Preloading and postloading were more common among respondents who had used ecstasy more than 50 times (preloading 55 against 30 in 100), among about 30 tests without correction. These figures describe one self-selected sample, not how common the practices are: respondents found through harm-reduction websites may be more interested in harm reduction, the response rate is unknown, the questionnaire was not validated, and how often each strategy was used was not asked. Whether any of these practices lowers harm was not studied: the authors note that the evidence that preloading protects comes only from studies in rodents given injected pre-treatments, and that taking 5-HTP, SSRI antidepressants or St John's wort with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome, which this survey did not examine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Allott & Redman (2006), n = 116: strategies to avoid negative side effects (from a list) drinking water 95.7%, limiting ecstasy 70.7%, breaks or 'chilling out' 62.1%, healthy lifestyle 59.5%, vitamins or natural products 52.6%, other illegal drugs 30.2%, prescription medications 15.5%; no strategy for the comedown 4.4%, for brain damage 18.1%. Pill testing: never 61.2%, rarely 16.4%, a quarter of the time 6%, half 1.7%, three quarters 8.6%, always 6% (ever 38.8%, editors' calculation). Preloaded 41.4%, postloaded 47.4%; preloading products (n = 46) multivitamins 50.0%, 5-HTP 41.3%, magnesium 23.9%, fruit or juice 23.9%; postloading (n = 54) 5-HTP 46.3%, multivitamins 44.4%, fruit or juice 24.1%; reasons (n = 55) to ease the comedown 45.5%, to reduce brain damage 32.7%, to reduce side effects 18.2%. Changed use because of dislikes 53% (61 people: 68.9% less often, 16.4% less per occasion, 13.1% stopped). Used before and during ecstasy: alcohol 91.4% and 81.0%, amphetamines 60.3% and 65.5%. Correlates (about 30 uncorrected tests): preloading with younger age (24.9 against 27.6 years, p = 0.011) and more than 50 occasions (54.7% against 30.2%, p = 0.007); postloading with more than 50 occasions (60.4% against 36.5%, p = 0.01) and monthly use (55.9% against 36.4%, p = 0.036). Editors' calculation: shares near 40–50% carry 95% intervals of about ±9 points.
